items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Function names are clear (openAfterSaleModal, submitCheckoutAction) and code is split into sections. But business-logic lambdas use single-letter names (`cartInfo.lines.forEach(l => ...)`, `order.refunds.reduce((sum, r) => ...)`, `ri`, `it`), which caps this at accept.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: Everything is in one new 2193-line index.html, which caps this at accept. UI handlers do route through shopTestAPI. However, clearCartAction changes shopState.cart directly, and openAfterSaleModal mixes HTML building with the refundable-quantity calculation.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: API failures return {ok:false,error} and are shown in toasts. But imported spec and name strings go into innerHTML unescaped, the after-sale qty uses parseInt with no NaN feedback, and 0.9 / thresholds look like magic constants.

items.name: Clerk workbench usability: amount breakdown, status hints, dangerous-action confirmation
items.name_zh: 店员工作台可用性：金额明细、状态提示与危险操作确认
items.evidence: Cancel, confirmReturn and reset ask for confirmation. Submitting an after-sale refund (submitAfterSaleAction), overwriting data on import (submitImportAction) and clearCartAction all run without any confirm. The checkout summary shows only the payable total, with no breakdown of each discount.

items.name: Business logic lives in one place (UI and test API share it; integer-cent money)
items.name_zh: 业务逻辑集中且被界面与测试接口共用（金额按分计算）
items.evidence: UI handlers call window.shopTestAPI.* (checkout, pay, requestAfterSale, importData), so the logic is shared. The visible money code uses floats with toFixed (order.payable.toFixed(2)), and the test asserted 71.1, so integer cents isn't evident. Hidden tests all failed.
